title: An End-to-End Hybrid Quantum--Classical Sampling Workflow for Discrete Markov Random Fields: A Reproducible Case Study
abstract: Sampling from discrete Markov random fields (MRFs) is a hard problem. We study amplitude-encoded i.i.d. sampling for small MRFs where $2^n$ target probabilities are precomputed classically. This removes quantum exponential speedup but allows a clean comparison against classical MCMC based on independent circuit samples ($τ\approx 1$). Across 60 instances spanning five graph families (1k-step burn-in, 3k retained samples), the mean ESS ratios of Quantum to Single-Site Gibbs, Block Gibbs, Tuned-Block, and Parallel Tempering are $16.35$, $7.29$, $1.82$, and $1.79$, showing modern classical samplers substantially close this gap. Amortizing $O(2^n)$ preprocessing into wall-clock time, exact inverse-CDF sampling yields $17.7\text{M}$ ESS/s versus $488\text{K}$ ESS/s for the quantum sampler ($36\times$ mean rate, $153\times$ per-instance), confirming no wall-clock advantage. We characterize MCMC autocorrelation costs and benchmark amplitude-encoded state preparation at $n \in \{8,10,12\}$. An MPS scaling study ($n \le 40$) shows bond dimension $χ=32$ achieves $F=0.721\pm0.059$ at $n=40$. Finally, a matched-budget VQC vs. MPS comparison at $n \in \{8,10,12\}$ shows VQC fidelities fall far below MPS: $(F_{\mathrm{VQC}}, F_{\mathrm{MPS}}) = (0.31, 0.99), (0.21, 0.96), (0.17, 0.88)$ at compressions $10.7\times$, $34.1\times$, and $113.8\times$.
summary: This paper rigorously benchmarks various sampling techniques—quantum amplitude encoding, VQC, and advanced classical MCMC—for estimating distributions from discrete Markov Random Fields. It finds that while quantum approaches show high theoretical ESS ratios, practical wall-clock comparisons reveal that state-of-the-art classical methods often match or exceed the performance when preprocessing costs are accounted for. The study concludes by cautioning against using shallow VQCs due to poor fidelity relative to established tensor network methods like MPS.
main_problem: The core problem is developing an efficient, scalable workflow for sampling from discrete Markov Random Fields (MRFs), which involves overcoming the exponential complexity associated with calculating partition functions.
main_result: While quantum amplitude encoding shows high Effective Sample Size (ESS) ratios compared to some classical samplers, advanced classical methods like inverse-CDF sampling significantly outperform it in wall-clock time when preprocessing costs are amortized. Furthermore, shallow Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC) were shown to underperform Matrix Product States (MPS) for approximating the distribution.
method: The work compares quantum amplitude encoding and VQC approaches against classical MCMC samplers (Gibbs variants, Parallel Tempering) and exact sampling techniques on MRFs.
model_or_system: The system is a discrete Markov Random Field defined over an undirected graph structure. The target probability distribution $P_{	heta}(\mathbf{x})$ is derived from the diagonal of a Hamiltonian, leading to $2^n$ amplitudes that must be sampled.
key_observables: Effective Sample Size (ESS) ratios, wall-clock ESS/s rates, Fidelity ($F$), Total Variation ($	ext{TV}$), and KL divergence ($D_{KL}$).
important_parameters: System size $n$ (up to 40 for MPS scaling), bond dimension $\chi$, and compression ratio.
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes that the classical preprocessing cost of $O(2^n)$ is amortized across all comparable methods, and VQC results are limited by shallow hardware-efficient ansätze.
figures_summary: Tables compare ESS ratios (Table I) showing quantum advantage narrowing as baselines improve; Table II compares wall-clock rates; Tables IV/IX show fidelity comparisons between VQC and MPS at increasing system sizes $n$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty of MRF sampling, then details amplitude encoding for small $n$ against classical MCMC. It proceeds to compare quantum vs. classical efficiency (ESS ratios), analyzes scaling limits using MPS fidelity, and concludes with a direct comparison showing VQC limitations relative to MPS.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it benchmarks the feasibility of using near-term quantum hardware for complex statistical inference problems common in condensed matter physics (e.g., phase transitions modeled by MRFs). The detailed benchmarking against classical state-of-the-art methods provides crucial guidance on when and how quantum resources might offer an advantage.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Experiment D: ESS ratio bar chart across all 60 instances, grouped by graph family, for single-site Gibbs, block Gibbs, and tuned-block Gibbs baselines. The ESS advantage is largest on bottleneck topologies (barbell, barbell-path) where Gibbs mixing is slowest. Tuned-block Gibbs substantially reduces the advantage (mean 1.82×) but does not eliminate it. Source: paper_table_metrics.json.

Fig. 2. Experiment D: ESS ratio (Quantum/Single-Site Gibbs) vs. mixing-difficulty proxy across 60 instances and 5 graph families. R2 = 0.00036, slope=0.688: family/topology effects dominate a sin- gle spectral-gap predictor. Mean ratio 16.35, range [8.24, 30.31]. Source: paper_table_metrics.json.

Fig. 3. Experiment B: VQC fidelity and compression ratio across n ∈ {6, . . . , 14} (source: reviewer_metrics.json), using the unconstrained depth-3 ansatz of Table VI, not the fixed-budget ansatz of Table IV. Compression grows from 1.8× at n = 6 to 195× at n = 14 at fixed depth d = 3, while fidelity plateaus near 0.44–0.49 for n ≥10, highlighting the fundamental tension between compression and approximation quality.

Fig. 4. Experiment A2: ∆F = Fclique −Flinear vs graph density across 36 matched (family, n, seed) instances (4 families × 3 sizes × 3 seeds). R2 = 0.0007, slope= −2.62 × 10−4: no detectable positive correlation between graph density and clique-entanglement benefit at n ≤14. Source: entanglement_sweep.json.
Fig. 5. Experiment A1: fidelity vs. n by entanglement strategy (linear, clique, full) across graph families. Clique-minus-linear mean ∆F = −2.28 × 10−4; full-minus-linear mean = +2.58 × 10−3.
